Third Servile War.aftermath:
The Fall of Spartacus
The rebels of the Third Servile War were annihilated by Crassus. Pompey's forces did not directly engage Spartacus's forces but his legions moving from the north were able to chase down some 5,000 rebels fleeing the battle, "all of whom he slew". After this action, Pompey sent a dispatch to the Senate, saying that while Crassus certainly had conquered the slaves in open battle, he, Pompey, had ended the war, thus claiming a large portion of the credit and earning the enmity of Crassus. While most of the rebel slaves were killed on the battlefield, some 6,000 survivors were captured by the legions of Crassus, all of whom were crucified along the Appian Way from Rome to Capua.

Torstenson War.aftermath:
The Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645. Brown: Denmark–Norway. Green: Sweden. Yellow: the provinces of Jämtland and Härjedalen plus Idre and Särna, and the Baltic Sea islands of Gotland and Ösel, which were ceded to Sweden. Red: the province of Halland, ceded for 30 years
Christian's Danish forces were so exhausted that he was forced to accept the mediation of France and the United Provinces in suing for peace. The Peace of Brömsebro was signed on 13 August 1645, a humiliating disaster to Denmark–Norway. The Swedes were exempted from the Sound Dues, the toll for passing through Danish territory into the Baltic Sea.

Uganda–Tanzania War.aftermath:
Analyses
Sociologist Ronald Aminzade asserted that "the key" to Tanzania's victory was its ideological framing of the war as a threat to the nation, thus facilitating the mobilisation of a popular militia that performed well in combat. Aminzade stated that in contrast Uganda "embarked on a nonideological territorial war", deploying forces that suffered from low morale and internal dissension. Journalist Godwin Matatu reasoned that the Uganda Army's failures rested on its low morale and reliance on vehicles and roads which made them vulnerable to Tanzanian ground forces, who travelled on foot for much of the war.

Ukrainian–Soviet War.outcome: First: Ukraine and Central Powers victory, Second: Soviet victory
Ukrainian–Soviet War.aftermath:
Eastern Europe after the Treaty of Riga
The end of the war saw the incorporation of most of the territories of Ukraine into the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic which, on December 30, 1922, was one of the founding members of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). Parts of Western Ukraine fell under the control of the Second Polish Republic, as laid out in the Peace of Riga. The UNR government, led by Symon Petlura, was forced into exile.
Ukrainian–Soviet War.keyTerms: Conflict dates: First: 8 November 191712 June 1918, Second: 2 January 1919November 1921

Venezuelan War of Independence.aftermath: The Spanish sent a fleet in 1823 to reconquer the country but were defeated at the Battle of Lake Maracaibo. In the following years Venezuelan forces, as part of the army of Gran Colombia, continued campaigning under the leadership of Bolívar to liberate the southern parts of New Granada and Ecuador. Once this was accomplished, Gran Colombia continued its fight against the Spanish in Peru and Bolivia, completing the efforts of Chilean and Argentine patriots, such as José de San Martín, who liberated southern South America.

Vietnam War.outcome: Fall of Saigon (30 April 1975) to North Vietnamese forces. North Vietnam, the Viet Cong, and their allies won.
Vietnam War.aftermath: Vietnam was unified under the communist government in Hanoi as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (1976). ~1 to 3 million Vietnamese died across two decades of war, plus ~58,000 American service members and significant losses in Laos and Cambodia. The Khmer Rouge took Cambodia in the same months and went on to kill ~1.5 to 2 million Cambodians. United States military and political confidence was deeply shaken, with effects on American foreign policy for a generation.
Vietnam War.keyTerms: Paris Peace Accords (27 January 1973) ended direct American involvement. The war between North and South Vietnam continued until Saigon fell on 30 April 1975 without a final treaty.
notable: Unification of Vietnam under the Hanoi government
Cambodian genocide under the Khmer Rouge (1975 to 1979)
Boat people exodus of refugees from Indochina
Lasting effect on American politics and military doctrine

War against the Islamic State.outcome: Coalition victory. The territorial caliphate declared by Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi in Mosul in June 2014 was destroyed by March 2019 with the fall of Baghouz, Syria. The organization persists as an insurgency and franchise.
War against the Islamic State.aftermath: Over five years of intense urban warfare reshaped Mosul, Raqqa, Fallujah, Ramadi, Tikrit, and other cities. The Syrian Democratic Forces, led by the Kurdish YPG, emerged as a US partner that strained the US–Turkey relationship for years after. Tens of thousands of civilians and combatants died. the displacement was on the scale of millions across Iraq and Syria. Baghdadi died in a US raid in Idlib (October 2019). ISIS affiliates remain active in West Africa, the Sahel, Afghanistan-Pakistan (ISIS-K), and elsewhere.
War against the Islamic State.keyTerms: No treaty. The end of the territorial caliphate was declared after the fall of Baghouz on 23 March 2019.
notable: Fall of Mosul to ISIS and the proclamation of the caliphate (June 2014)
Battles of Kobani (2014–2015) and the rise of the SDF
Battle of Mosul (2016–2017) and Battle of Raqqa (2017)
Death of Baghdadi in Idlib (October 2019)
Ongoing insurgency in Syria's Badia and northern Iraq

War in Afghanistan (2001–2021).outcome: Taliban victory. The US-backed Afghan government collapsed on 15 August 2021 as the Taliban entered Kabul. The final American withdrawal completed 30 August 2021.
War in Afghanistan (2001–2021).aftermath: Twenty years and an estimated 176,000 deaths, including ~2,400 US service members and tens of thousands of Afghan security forces and civilians. The United States spent over two trillion dollars. The Taliban reimposed restrictive social policy, particularly affecting women and girls. The departure created a refugee outflow of hundreds of thousands. Al-Qaeda's central leadership was severely degraded over the war but reconstituted in different geographies. ISIS-K emerged as a competitor. NATO's first and longest combat deployment ended without a treaty.
War in Afghanistan (2001–2021).keyTerms: Doha Agreement (29 February 2020) between the United States and the Taliban set the conditions for US withdrawal. No agreement with the Afghan government.
notable: Initial defeat of the Taliban government (October–November 2001)
Battle of Tora Bora and bin Laden's escape (December 2001)
Operation Anaconda (March 2002), first large conventional US ground action
Surge and counterinsurgency strategy (2009–2012)
Fall of Kabul and the Kabul Airport evacuation (August 2021)

War in Iraq (2013–2017).aftermath: Months of relative calm in Baghdad ended with over 27 people killed by suicide bombers over a period of 3 days in mid-January 2018. Although there were no immediate claims of responsibility, it was reported that such attacks had usually been the work of the jihadist group Islamic State (IS) in the past, and that elements of the group were still active north of the city despite the government's claim of victory in December 2017. On Wednesday January 17, two days after the two suicide bombings on January 15, IS "claimed responsibility for the twin suicide bombings in Baghdad this week", though the New York Times suggested that the delay, and a number of errors in the claim, may show that the group's "media apparatus has been disrupted".

War of 1812.outcome: Treaty of Ghent (24 December 1814) restored the pre-war borders. The war ended in a stalemate, though both sides claimed victory.
War of 1812.aftermath: United States borders with British North America were unchanged. The Battle of New Orleans (8 January 1815) was fought after the treaty was signed but before news reached the parties. Native American confederations in the Northwest and the South lost their most effective resistance to American expansion. Britain shifted its colonial focus toward what would become Canada.
War of 1812.keyTerms: Treaty of Ghent (24 December 1814), restoring status quo ante bellum.
notable: Burning of Washington by British forces (August 1814)
Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans (January 1815)
End of organized Native resistance east of the Mississippi
Beginning of nearly two centuries of unguarded United States to Canada border

War of the Confederation.aftermath: General Bulnes again assumed the initiative. After the defeat of the Confederate army at Yungay on January 20, the Chileans commenced a second push southward, occupying Lima for the second time in April. Santa Cruz had already fled to Ecuador, and both the war and the short-lived Peru-Bolivian Confederation now came to an end.

War of the Fifth Coalition.aftermath:
The Battle of Znaim was the last action between Austria and France in the War of the Fifth Coalition
After the main Austrian force was defeated at Wagram, the nation's forces collapsed, according to historian Charles Esdaile, and Emperor Francis was forced to sue for peace. Englund attributes the end to "diplomatic considerations" and believes that Austria could have continued to fight. The Treaty of Schönbrunn, signed on 14 October 1809, imposed a heavy political toll on the Austrians. Metternich and Charles succeeded in negotiating lighter terms in return for Austrian co-operation and most of the hereditary Habsburg territories were preserved.

War of the First Coalition.outcome: French victory. Treaty of The Hague, Treaty of Paris, Peaces of Basel, Treaty of Tolentino, Treaty of Campo Formio

War of the Fourth Coalition.aftermath:
Prussia (orange) and its territories lost at Tilsit (other colours)
Following the Treaties of Tilsit, Britain and Sweden remained the only two major coalition members still at war with France. Russia soon declared war against Britain and after a British attack on Copenhagen, Denmark–Norway joined the war on the side of Napoleon (Gunboat War), opening a second front against Sweden. A short British expedition under Sir John Moore was sent to Sweden (May 1808) to protect against any possible Franco-Danish invasion.

War of the League of Cambrai.aftermath: The Triumph of Venice (oil on canvas by Pompeo Batoni, 1737) depicts Leonardo Loredan, Doge of Venice during the war.

War of the Portuguese Succession.aftermath: The combined Spanish-Portuguese navy's victory resulted in the rapid conquest of the Azores, completing the dynastic union of the Portuguese and Spanish empires. The King Philip II of Spain was recognized as King Philip I of Portugal and of the Algarves by the Portuguese Cortes of Tomar (1581). In 1589, António made an attempt on Lisbon supported by English forces under the command of Sir Francis Drake and Sir John Norreys. When the people failed to rise and yield the city to Dom António, the attempt was abandoned. Spain and Portugal would remain united in a dynastic union of the crowns (remaining formally independent and with autonomous administrations) for the next 60 years, until 1640. This union is called the Iberian Union.

War of the Quadruple Alliance.aftermath: The war provided a unique example during the eighteenth century in which Britain and France were on the same side. It came during a period between 1716 and 1731, when the two countries were allies. Spain would later join with France in the Bourbon Compact, and the two would become enemies of the British once more. Spain later regained the Kingdom of Naples during the 1733 to 1735 War of the Polish Succession.

War of the Second Coalition.aftermath: On 25 March 1802, Britain and France signed the Treaty of Amiens, ending British involvement in the war. After a preliminary treaty signed at Paris on 9 October 1801, the Treaty of Paris of 25 June 1802 ended the war between France and the Ottoman Empire, the last remaining member of the Second Coalition. The peace treaties ceded the left bank of the Rhine to France and recognized the independence of the Cisalpine, Batavian and Helvetic republics. Thus began the longest period of peace during the period 1792–1815.

War of the Sicilian Vespers.outcome: Peace of Caltabellotta, House of Barcelona gains Sicilian throne
War of the Sicilian Vespers.aftermath: The war, fought between Christian powers over claims to European thrones, is seen by some sources as a sign of the end of the Crusading era, and an indicative sign of the degradation of papal powers over excommunication and indulgence.

War of the Sixth Coalition.aftermath: Napoleon was determined to fight on, proposing to march on Paris. His soldiers and regimental officers were eager to fight on. But Napoleon's marshals and senior officers mutinied. On 4 April, at Fontainebleau, Napoleon was confronted by his marshals and senior officers, led by Ney. They told the Emperor that they refused to march. Napoleon asserted that the army would follow him. Ney replied, "the army will obey its chiefs".

War of the Spanish Succession.outcome: Treaties of Utrecht, Rastatt, and Baden

Austerlitz and the preceding campaign profoundly altered the nature of European politics. In three months, the French had occupied Vienna, decimated two armies, and humbled the Austrian Empire. These events sharply contrast with the rigid power structures of the 18th century, when no major European capital was ever held by an enemy army. Austerlitz set the stage for a near-decade of French domination on the European continent, but one of its more immediate impacts was to goad Prussia into war in 1806.

Wars in Lombardy.outcome: Treaty of Lodi, compromise treaty leading to a balance of power and a period of stability

Wars of the Diadochi.keyTerms: Conflict dates: 322–281 BC (41 years) (struggle over Macedon ended in 272 BC)

Wars of the Three Kingdoms.aftermath: Having defeated all organised opposition, the Grandees of the Parliamentary New Model Army and their civilian supporters dominated the politics of all three nations for the next nine years (see Interregnum (1649–1660)). As for England, the Rump Parliament had already decreed it was a republic and a Commonwealth. Ireland and Scotland were now subjugated and ruled by military governors, and constituent representatives from both nations were seated in the Rump Parliament of the Protectorate, where they were dominated by Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector. When Cromwell died in 1658, control of the Commonwealth became unstable.

World War I.outcome: Armistice of Compiègne (11 November 1918, 11:00) ended fighting on the Western Front. The Allies (France, United Kingdom, United States, Italy, Russia until 1917) won.
World War I.aftermath: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed reparations and territorial losses on Germany. The Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, Russian, and German empires all collapsed and were replaced by republics or new states. ~20 million people died, roughly half of them civilians. The 1918 influenza pandemic, accelerated by wartime troop movement, killed another ~50 million. The League of Nations was founded but proved unable to prevent the next war.
World War I.keyTerms: Armistice (11 November 1918) followed by the Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919), Treaty of Saint-Germain (Austria), Treaty of Trianon (Hungary), Treaty of Sèvres / Lausanne (Ottoman Empire).
notable: Collapse of four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, Ottoman)
Creation of Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and the Baltic states
Mandate system divides the former Ottoman lands
Russian Revolution removed Russia from the war in 1917

World War II.outcome: Unconditional surrender of Germany (8 May 1945) and Japan (2 September 1945). The Allies (Soviet Union, United States, United Kingdom, China, France) won.
World War II.aftermath: Germany was occupied and partitioned into four zones, which became West Germany and East Germany. Japan was occupied by the United States until 1952. ~70 to 85 million people died, roughly 3 percent of the 1940 world population. The Holocaust killed ~6 million Jews and ~5 million others. The United Nations replaced the League of Nations, the Bretton Woods system reshaped global finance, and the Soviet Union and United States emerged as the two postwar superpowers. The trial of Nazi leaders at Nuremberg established the precedent that aggressive war and crimes against humanity are individually prosecutable.
World War II.keyTerms: Unconditional surrender. Signed at Reims (7 May), ratified at Karlshorst (8 May) for Germany. Signed aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay (2 September) for Japan.
notable: Nuremberg and Tokyo war crimes trials
Partition of Germany and creation of the United Nations
Start of the nuclear age following Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Beginning of the Cold War

Yom Kippur War.aftermath: Analyses differ on the military outcome of the war. as an Israeli victory by some military historians,}} an Egyptian victory by other historians, and by others, as a military stalemate.

northern front of the Russian invasion o.aftermath: After Ukraine had fully retaken Kyiv Oblast, its military began to mop up pockets of isolated Russian troops who had been left behind in the retreat. The Institute for the Study of War assessed that these remnant groups did not offer organized resistance. The Institute for the Study of War also said that some of the Russian units that were pulled back to Belarus and western Russia would "remain combat ineffective for a protracted period".

transition from Sui to Tang.outcome: China united by the Tang dynasty
